section_summary: Pages 73-75 conclude a Chungking-produced translation of an interview on Japan’s wartime food policy, covering household cultivation, seed distribution, rationing, substitute foods, centralized distribution, and emergency preparations for air raids. Page 76 is a brief Department of State note comparing an unnamed observer’s relatively optimistic assessment with that of Mr. Plowman of the Otis Elevator Company.

subfiles.title: Interview on Japanese wartime food policy and “decisive battle” food distribution (continued)
subfiles.about: Japanese officials discuss cultivation, rationing, substitute staples, centralized distribution, and emergency food arrangements during air raids.
subfiles.summary: The interviewee urges households to cultivate unused land and explains that most seeds are available, although potato and sweet-potato seed supplies are lacking. Government ration plans allocate necessities by prefecture and supplement shortages with products such as bean malt, bean curd, greens, and canned food. The discussion then traces the public’s adaptation to wheat, sweet potatoes, noodles, bread, and mixed foods as rice supplies declined during the war. Officials also claim that emergency distribution and air-defense measures have been prepared, while encouraging families to maintain their own food reserves.

subfiles.title: Note comparing reports on conditions in Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State, Adviser on Political Relations
subfiles.about: A brief note states that an unnamed observer presents a more optimistic picture than Mr. Plowman’s recent account.
subfiles.summary: The Adviser on Political Relations records that the present observer gives a much brighter picture than the one received the previous day from Mr. Plowman of the Otis Elevator Company. The note clarifies that Plowman had recently traveled from Japan to the United States, rather than in the opposite direction.
